hindi: द्वारा परिभाषित है। तब $F\left(-\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\right)$ का मान ______ है।
solution: $1-t^{2}+t^{4}>0$, so the integrand is continuous and $F$ is continuous and odd with $F'=\frac{1+t^{2}}{1-t^{2}+t^{4}}$ (FTC)
So $F(x)=\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{1-x^{2}}$ on $(-1,1)$ and $F(x)=\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{1-x^{2}}-\pi$ for $x<-1$ (continuity at $-1$: left limit of $\tan^{-1}$ is $\frac{\pi}{2}$, $F(-1)=-\frac{\pi}{2}$)
solution_full: $1-t^{2}+t^{4}=\left(t^{2}-\frac12\right)^{2}+\frac34>0$, so the integrand is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$. By the first part of the fundamental theorem, $F$ is differentiable with $F'(x)=\dfrac{1+x^{2}}{1-x^{2}+x^{4}}$; $F$ is odd since the integrand is even.

For $x\neq\pm1$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{1-x^{2}}=\dfrac{1+x^{2}}{(1-x^{2})^{2}+x^{2}}=\dfrac{1+x^{2}}{1-x^{2}+x^{4}}$. So $\phi(x)=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{1-x^{2}}$ is an antiderivative on each of $(-\infty,-1)$, $(-1,1)$, $(1,\infty)$, but not across $\pm1$.
On $(-1,1)$, $F$ and $\phi$ have the same derivative and $F(0)=\phi(0)=0$, so $F=\phi$ there. As $x\to-1^{+}$, $\frac{x}{1-x^{2}}\to-\infty$, so $F(-1)=-\frac{\pi}{2}$ (by continuity of $F$).
On $(-\infty,-1)$, $F=\phi+C$. As $x\to-1^{-}$, $\frac{x}{1-x^{2}}\to+\infty$ and $\phi\to\frac{\pi}{2}$. Continuity of $F$ at $-1$ gives $\frac{\pi}{2}+C=-\frac{\pi}{2}$, so $C=-\pi$.
Hence $F(x_0)=\tan^{-1}1-\pi=\frac{\pi}{4}-\pi=-\frac{3\pi}{4}=-2.356\ldots$, which is $-2.36$ to two decimal places. (The naive value $\phi(x_0)-\phi(0)=\frac{\pi}{4}$ ignores the jump.)

Cross-check: $\frac{1+t^{2}}{1-t^{2}+t^{4}}=\frac12\left[\frac{1}{t^{2}+\sqrt3t+1}+\frac{1}{t^{2}-\sqrt3t+1}\right]$ gives the continuous antiderivative $\tan^{-1}(2x+\sqrt3)+\tan^{-1}(2x-\sqrt3)$, whose value at $x_0$ is also $-\frac{3\pi}{4}$.
originality_note: New: the evaluation point is chosen beyond the jump of the natural antiderivative tan^-1(x/(1-x^2)) and exactly where its argument equals 1, so the naive answer pi/4 is wrong and the correct one is -3 pi/4 (way 4). Closest known: the textbook trap int_{-1}^{1} d/dx(tan^-1(1/x)) dx. Different because: the function is an integral function evaluated at a golden-ratio point and continuity of F must be used to fix the constant.
blueprint_concepts: Evaluation via the antiderivative; handling discontinuous antiderivatives

concept_use.Evaluation via the antiderivative; handl: tan^-1(x/(1-x^2)) is an antiderivative only on intervals avoiding x = +-1; a constant -pi must be added for x < -1.
concept_use.Fundamental theorem of calculus (both pa: F(x) = int_0^x is continuous with F' = integrand (part 1), and continuity of F fixes the constant on (-inf, -1).

stem_review: Read as a student: F has domain/codomain; integrand continuous; evaluation point explicit. Checked by mpmath quadrature: F(x0) = -2.35619 = -3pi/4. Answer -2.36 (negative decimal, clearly rounded). Changed: No change.
key_step: The antiderivative tan^-1(x/(1-x^2)) jumps at x = -1; continuity of F forces F = tan^-1(x/(1-x^2)) - pi for x < -1.
justification: Two linked ideas (FTC continuity of an integral function, and recognising the jump of the antiderivative) with a numerical answer. Same demand as 2024-P2-Q13 (L3) on piecewise antiderivatives.
